strengths: The paper tackles an important and timely problem: controllable robot video/world generation with finer spatial grounding than action-only or text-only conditioning. The idea of using 4D semantic occupancy as an intermediate representation is well motivated for robot manipulation, where geometry, depth, and object identity matter for plausible interaction dynamics.

The system is broad and technically ambitious: it includes an occupancy curation pipeline, a CogVideoX-based action and visual conditioning model, a multi-view extension, and a sim-to-real use case. The manuscript provides useful implementation detail in the appendix, including architecture changes, preprocessing, training cost, and hyperparameters.

The main single-view quantitative results are reasonably strong. On BridgeV2 and RT-1, ORV improves substantially over reported baselines on PSNR/SSIM and FVD, and the ablation on BridgeV2 shows that depth and semantic occupancy cues improve over action-only conditioning.

The work has potential practical value for robotics datasets and simulation, especially if the occupancy conditioning can be produced reliably from simulators or sensors. The multi-view and sim-to-real demonstrations are promising directions.
weaknesses: The central evidence is not fully aligned with several of the strongest claims. The paper claims improved controllability, multi-view consistency, and sim-to-real transfer, but quantitative evaluation is largely limited to standard video reconstruction metrics. There are no direct action-following/control-precision metrics, no physical-consistency metrics, no multi-view consistency metrics, and no downstream robot policy or imitation-learning evaluation.

The evaluation protocol for occupancy conditioning is insufficiently clear and may make comparisons to action-only baselines unfair. The method receives rendered depth/semantic condition maps derived from 4D occupancy, while baselines appear to receive only actions or weaker controls. It is unclear how much future scene/object motion is encoded in these condition maps during validation, especially when occupancy is curated from the full target video. If the conditioning contains target-future geometry, PSNR/SSIM/FVD gains do not by themselves establish better generative dynamics or action controllability.

The occupancy curation pipeline is complex and depends on many pretrained systems (Qwen-VL, Grounding DINO, SAM2, Monst3R, NKSR, clustering and voting), but the paper does not evaluate the accuracy of the resulting semantic occupancy, failure modes, or sensitivity to reconstruction/segmentation errors. Since this representation is the core contribution, the lack of quantitative validation of occupancy quality is a material gap.

The multi-view contribution is weakly supported. ORV-MV is shown qualitatively, but there is no baseline comparison, no quantitative cross-view consistency metric, and no analysis of camera/view generalization. The method also requires multi-view first-frame observations, which limits the claimed utility for building 4D worlds from sparse input.

The sim-to-real section is mostly a qualitative demonstration. There is no comparison to alternative sim-to-real rendering/domain adaptation approaches, no measurement of realism beyond visual examples, and no evidence that generated videos improve real robot learning or transfer. The phrase 'effectively narrowing the domain gap' is therefore stronger than the evidence supports.

Baseline coverage and fairness are uneven: several entries are unavailable on major datasets, and the manuscript does not clearly specify whether baselines were retrained under comparable data, resolution, input context, action representation, and compute. Some reported FID/FVD behavior is mixed, e.g. ORV is not best on all FID columns, but the narrative sometimes overstates consistent superiority.

Reproducibility is only partial. Training details are extensive, but the data curation process has many underspecified prompt/model/configuration choices and large storage/compute requirements. The first page advertises demo/code/model but no actual link is visible in the manuscript text, making the reproducibility claim hard to assess from the submission alone.

Presentation is generally understandable but has a number of clarity issues and overclaims. Some sections contain awkward or imprecise wording, table references appear inconsistent, and key distinctions such as 'Recon.' versus 'Render' conditioning are not explained enough for a reader to judge the experimental setting confidently.

strengths: The paper addresses an important problem: controllable robot manipulation video generation, where better geometric and semantic conditioning could be useful for simulation, data augmentation, and downstream robot learning.

The core idea of using 4D semantic occupancy as an intermediate control representation is plausible and relevant. The pipeline attempts to connect reconstruction, semantic labeling, Gaussian-style rendering of condition maps, and a pretrained video generator in a coherent system.

The single-view quantitative results report clear gains over several baselines on BridgeV2, Droid, and RT-1, especially on BridgeV2 and RT-1 PSNR/SSIM/FVD. The ablation in Table 3 suggests that depth and semantic occupancy conditions both contribute beyond action-only conditioning.

The manuscript includes nontrivial engineering detail: dataset curation, action injection into AdaLN, visual condition fusion, multi-view attention, training schedules, preprocessing settings, and compute requirements are described more concretely than many generative-video submissions.
weaknesses: The main experimental comparison appears unfair or at least under-specified. ORV is compared against action/text/video baselines while receiving additional future visual condition sequences derived from 4D occupancy. For real validation data, these occupancy-derived condition maps seem to be reconstructed from the target videos themselves, which may leak future geometry and object motion. This makes the reported gains hard to interpret as better action-conditioned video prediction rather than image/video translation from privileged controls.

The central claim of improved controllability is not directly evaluated. The paper relies mainly on PSNR, SSIM, FID, and FVD, which do not measure action adherence, contact correctness, object trajectory accuracy, physical plausibility, or task success. No downstream robot learning result is provided, despite repeated claims that the generated videos benefit policy learning or imitation learning.

The multi-view and sim-to-real extensions are weakly supported. ORV-MV and ORV-S2R are presented as major contributions, but the evidence is almost entirely qualitative. There are no quantitative cross-view consistency metrics, no camera-pose or 3D reconstruction evaluation, no sim-to-real task success, and no comparison to relevant sim-to-real or multi-view generation baselines.

The method depends on a very heavy and fragile curation pipeline using VLM captioning, Grounding DINO, SAM2 tracking, Monst3R, NKSR, VGGT, clustering, voxelization, and Gaussian rendering. Errors in any stage could strongly affect the final supervision, but the paper does not evaluate occupancy quality, semantic labeling accuracy, tracking failures, reconstruction failures, or sensitivity to these components.

The practical usefulness is overstated. If future occupancy sequences must be available at inference, the model is less a general robot world model and more a renderer/translator from precomputed dynamics. If occupancy comes from a simulator, the contribution should be evaluated as sim-conditioned video synthesis, but the paper does not establish that this improves over simpler rendering, domain randomization, ControlNet-style conditioning, or other geometry-conditioned diffusion baselines.

The baseline coverage is incomplete and not always matched. Some entries are missing for datasets, and the comparisons do not clearly control for backbone, training data, conditioning strength, or fine-tuning budget. The paper claims ControlNet-like conditioning has comparable performance in the supplement, but no clear quantitative ControlNet comparison is included in the main results.

Reproducibility is limited. The manuscript says demo/code/model are available, but the link appears blank in the extracted text. The pipeline requires large compute and storage, including about 8TB for BridgeV2 curation and 8 H100 training, and many empirical hyperparameters. Without released curated occupancy data and scripts, reproducing the results would be difficult.

The writing and presentation contain many rough edges: grammatical issues, inconsistent terminology, vague claims such as “seamlessly” and “physically grounded,” table-reference mistakes, and unclear descriptions of what information is available at training versus inference. These are not merely cosmetic because they obscure the actual problem setting and fairness of evaluation.

strengths: The paper proposes a well-motivated representation choice: using 4D semantic occupancy as an intermediate, spatially aligned control signal for robot video generation. This is a plausible and useful bridge between coarse action conditioning and pixel-level video synthesis, especially for manipulation where object geometry and contact matter.

The system is broad and practically interesting. ORV covers single-view action-conditioned generation, an extension to multi-view generation, and a simulation-to-real use case, all built on a modern pretrained video backbone. The pipeline for curating pseudo 4D semantic occupancy from BridgeV2, Droid, and RT-1 is also a meaningful engineering contribution.

The main quantitative results are encouraging. On BridgeV2 and RT-1, ORV improves substantially over CogVideoX, HMA, and IRASim on PSNR/SSIM/FVD, and it also improves FVD on Droid. The ablations show that depth and semantic occupancy conditions contribute beyond action-only conditioning, and that pretrained CogVideoX is important.

The supplementary material provides useful implementation detail: dataset processing, occupancy voxelization/rendering settings, action/AdaLN integration, multiview training sampling, evaluation sample size, and compute cost. This helps reproducibility relative to many large generative robotics papers.

The qualitative examples are consistent with the paper's thesis: occupancy guidance appears to improve object/gripper motion fidelity and multi-view geometric consistency in cases where action-only baselines struggle.
weaknesses: The evidence for two major claimed capabilities, multi-view generation and sim-to-real transfer, is mostly qualitative. ORV-MV is shown with examples but lacks quantitative cross-view consistency, 3D reconstruction quality, camera-pose consistency, or downstream policy-learning evaluation. ORV-S2R is demonstrated with a single-style qualitative transfer and no real robot or policy metric, so the claim of reducing the sim-to-real gap is not fully established.

The evaluation is still centered on image/video reconstruction metrics such as PSNR, SSIM, FID, and FVD. These are useful but do not directly measure whether generated videos improve robot learning, policy generalization, contact correctness, or physical plausibility. Since the motivation is scalable robot simulation/data synthesis, the absence of a downstream robotics experiment is a notable limitation.

The occupancy curation pipeline depends on several large pretrained components, including VLM captioning, Grounding DINO, SAM2, Monst3R, and NKSR. The paper does not sufficiently quantify the accuracy or failure modes of the generated semantic occupancy labels, even though errors in this pseudo ground truth could strongly affect both training and evaluation.

Some comparisons are incomplete or uneven. Several baselines are unavailable on some datasets, and the paper does not compare quantitatively against some closely related/concurrent geometry-conditioned robotic video transfer or 4D world-model methods. It is therefore hard to isolate how much of the gain comes from occupancy guidance versus backbone/training/data scale choices.

The generalization evidence is suggestive but limited. The paper claims in-domain, out-of-domain, appearance, and trajectory adaptation, yet these are mostly visual demonstrations without systematic splits, quantitative OOD metrics, or stress tests for unseen objects, viewpoints, lighting, embodiment changes, and longer-horizon rollouts.

Reproducibility remains costly and somewhat fragile despite good implementation details. The full pipeline requires an 8xH100 setup and very large curated intermediate storage, e.g. around 8TB for BridgeV2, which may limit independent reproduction. There are also some presentation issues and inconsistencies, such as references to the wrong table number, typos, and unclear wording around Gaussian scaling parameters.
